en: BhG 1.1 Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: On the field of righteousness, the field of the Kurus, they have assembled, desiring to fight.
What did my sons and the Pāṇḍavas do, O Saṃjaya? //1//
I bow to Mādhava, the supreme bliss, who wondrously possesses the skill to explain all remaining and non-remaining doctrines from his single mouth, just as Śrīdhara does.
Having respectfully bowed to Śrī Mādhava, the Lord of the Universe,
and being constrained by devotion to Him, I compose this easy-to-understand commentary on the Gītā.
Having carefully examined the views of the author of the Bhāṣya as well as the words of its commentators according to my own understanding, I shall commence this commentary on the Gītā.
This Subodhinī commentary, by the mere effort of whose recitation the Gītā is explained, should always be meditated upon by the wise.

In this world, indeed, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, who has descended for the welfare of the entire world and is supremely compassionate, rescued Arjuna— from whom discernment had been lost due to grief and delusion brought about by ignorance of reality, and who, having abandoned his own duty, was intent upon the duties of others— by means of the raft of instruction in the secret of the knowledge of Dharma, from that ocean of grief and delusion.
Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana composed that very subject matter taught by the Blessed One in seven hundred verses; therein,
he wrote down almost all the verses as they actually issued from the mouth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
while composing a few himself for the sake of connecting them.
As it is said in the *Gītā-māhātmya*:
"The *Gītā* should be well-sung; what is the use of other extensive scriptures, since it has issued forth directly from the lotus-mouth of Padmanābha himself?"

In this regard, from the passage beginning with "On that field of dharma" up to the end of the section ending with "despondent, he spoke thus," the narrative is presented as an introduction to the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna;
thereafter, until the conclusion, follows their dialogue for the purpose of understanding dharma and knowledge.
There, with the verse beginning "Dharmakṣetre," etc., Dhṛtarāṣṭra questioned his charioteer Sañjaya—
who was standing nearby at Hastināpura— regarding the events at Kurukṣetra; and although Sañjaya remained in Hastināpura,
having obtained divine vision through the grace of Vyāsa, he reported the events of Kurukṣetra to Dhṛtarāṣṭra as if seeing them directly.
Having seen the Pandava army, etc.,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"On the field of dharma," and so forth.
O Sañjaya!
On Kurukṣetra, the field of dharma, the ground of righteousness;
"field of dharma" is an epithet for Kurukṣetra.
Among these, there was a certain first progenitor named Kuru.

At Kuru’s seat of dharma, my sons—the sons of Māmakī—and the sons of Pāṇḍu, desiring to fight and wishing for battle, assembled and met together; what did they do? What did they perform?—[thus asks] Viśvanātha.
Clad in white silken garments, delighting the noble night-lotuses, dispelling the darkness of the cowherds by his own splendor— he, the ocean of nectar Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya, is mine.
Presiding over the mind, may he grant us beautiful speech.
Having thoroughly reflected upon the words of the ancients, I—
though ignorant and desiring only a mere drop of the nectar of the Gītā— here follow the very opinion of my lord, the Yati.
O peaceful ones, forgive me, who have come to you for refuge.
Indeed, here the Lord Himself— the son of Śrī Vasudeva, who is the Supreme Brahman in human form and whose worship of the lotus feet of the venerable masters esteemed by all scriptures is well-known—
having descended directly in the city of Śrī Gopāla, made Himself an object of perception for the eyes of all people through His boundless and supremely inconceivable worldly manifestation;
and having rescued the people of the world who were sinking in the ocean of existence, He immersed them in His own great ocean of love by means of the tasting of His own beauty and sweetness.
Although he was firmly established in the greatest vow of protecting the virtuous and subduing the wicked, under the pretext of removing the burden and suffering of the earth,

he performed only the supreme protection characterized by granting liberation— even to the wicked, even to his own haters, and even to those swallowed up in the great cycle of saṃsāra— thereby [protecting] those who, after his own disappearance, would be born afflicted by grief, delusion, and other passions bound by the fetters of beginningless ignorance.
Furthermore, in order to uplift living beings and to preserve His own dear friend— whose fame is sung by hosts of sages who composed the scriptures— the Lord,

by the power of His own will, directed the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā scripture toward Arjuna at the forefront of the battle; this scripture consists of three divisions and is adorned with the jewels of the ultimate meaning that culminates the purport of all the Vedas.
The eighteenth chapter manifested the supreme human goal— which contains within it the eighteen branches of knowledge— as if making it directly present;
therein, by the first group of six chapters, the yoga of desireless action is established.
By the second [verse], bhakti-yoga is shown;
by the third, jñāna-yoga is indicated.
Even among those, bhakti-yoga is placed in the middle because it is the most secret, because it is the most honored as that which revives both paths, and because it is the most difficult to attain.
Since both action and knowledge are rendered useless by the absence of devotion, those two are accepted only when mixed with devotion.
Devotion, moreover, is of two kinds: pure and predominant.
Of these, the former is intrinsically and supremely powerful.
Those two—action and knowledge—are, by themselves, pure in power, devoid of anything else, and denoted by such terms as "without-a-second" (*ananyādi*).
However, the second [form] is a mixture of action and knowledge; all of this will be explained in detail further on.

Now, in response to the inquiry as to what kind of grief and delusion Arjuna possessed, the venerable Vaiśampāyana, the narrator of the *Mahābhārata*, introduces the story to Janamejaya in the *Bhīṣma-parvan*:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Thus—tell me what those on my side, Duryodhana and the others, and the Pāṇḍavas, Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, did when they had assembled at Kurukṣetra, desiring to fight for the sake of battle.

Now, you yourself have stated that they were 'desirous of fighting' (yuyutsavaḥ); therefore, they were already prepared to engage in combat. With what intention, then, do you ask what else they did? To this, [the Lord] says: 'On the field of dharma...'"
According to the Vedic revelation that "Kurukṣetra is the sacrificial ground of the gods," it is well known that this field is a promoter of righteousness (*dharma*).
Therefore, by the power of association with that place, even unrighteous men such as Duryodhana and others might develop a mind inclined toward *dharma* through the cessation of their anger.
Since the Pāṇḍavas, however, are righteous by their very nature, the slaughter of their kinsmen would be improper; thus, when discernment arises in both parties, peace (*sandhi*) is also possible.

Therefore, my external desire is to make Sañjaya understand that "it shall be mine alone, O Ānanda. But internally, since peace has been reached, the kingdom remains as before—full of thorns—for my sons; thus, my despair is indeed difficult to restrain.
Consequently, since our Bhīṣma is truly invincible by Arjuna, war alone is better; yet the thought that "let it be so" is merely a wish for his [Arjuna's] benefit, which is difficult to perceive.

Here, by the word "field" (*kṣetra*) in the phrase "in this field of Dharma," the Dharma—the entryway to righteousness along with its attendants, Yudhiṣṭhira—is likened to a grain storehouse; Śrī Kṛṣṇa, its protector, is likened to the strength of the plowman;
and the various kinds of assistance rendered by Kṛṣṇa are likened to the watering of crops, the building of embankments, and so forth.

And Sarasvatī has made it understood that Duryodhana and others, who were to be eliminated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, stood in the place of specific types of grass that resemble grain but are actually hostile to it. //1//
Baladeva—He who possesses the singular side of true, infinite, and inconceivable power; the sovereign over all; and supremely skillful in protecting His devotees.
May my mind remain eternally fixed upon Śrī Govinda, who is the source of the creation and other processes of the universe, and who is perfect bliss.
By which the ocean of ignorance reaches its end,
supreme devotion attains its highest nourishment,
and even that most difficult-to-perceive supreme reality shines forth incessantly— [that is this knowledge].
I bow to the Gītā composed by Him who possesses the sixfold excellence.

Then the Blessed Lord Himself— the mass of blissful consciousness, the Supreme Person of inconceivable power, whose feet are meditated upon by Brahmā and others, and who brings about the diverse arising and dissolution of the universe through His own will—

desiring to gladden His own attendants who had manifested alongside Him in the pastimes of His birth and so forth, and wishing to liberate many living beings from the mouth of the tigress of ignorance by that very means, and desiring to uplift others who would appear after His own disappearance, spoke thus at the forefront of the battle.

Although Arjuna was His very own self, the Lord, by means of His inconceivable power, made him appear as if bewildered; then, under the pretext of clearing away that bewilderment, He imparted His own Gītā-Upaniṣad, which uniquely defines the true nature of His own self along with its attendants.
In that work, indeed, five subjects are described: the Lord, the individual soul, primordial nature, time, and karma.
Among these, the Lord is the all-pervasive consciousness;
the individual soul is the atomic consciousness;
and primordial nature (prakṛti) is the substance that serves as the substratum for the three qualities, beginning with sattva.
Time is an insentient substance devoid of the three guṇas;
action is that which is produced by human effort and is denoted by such terms as "adṛṣṭa" (the unseen force) and so forth.
These are their definitions.
Among these, the four beginning with Īśvara are eternal; those beginning with the individual soul (jīva), however, are subject to the control of Īśvara;
while karma is beginningless like antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) and yet perishable.

In this regard, although the Lord and the individual soul (jīva) have consciousness as their essential nature, they are the cognizer and the object "I"— as expressed in such passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," "He who is all-knowing,
all-perceiving," and "The person who is the thinker, the perceiver, the agent, and the self-conscious one."
Thus says the Śruti; and from such Śruti passages as:
"He desired, 'May I be many,'" and "I slept happily, I was not conscious of anything," and so forth.
Nor does this ego (ahaṅkāra) arise from the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva) in both cases,
because at that time it has not yet arisen and has already dissolved;
and he [the Self] is established as the agent, the enjoyer, the omniscient, and the all-knowing, based on the scriptural terms "agent," "knower," "doer," and "awakened one."
Indeed, the state of being an experiencer is universally accepted as the state of being an enjoyer;
this is made perfectly clear for both [the individual soul and Brahman] by the Śruti text: "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman.

Although the nature of being a cognizer and so forth is not distinct from the very nature of consciousness—just as the nature of being an illuminator is not distinct from the nature of light of the sun—yet...
Nevertheless, due to the efficacy of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), there is the conventional usage of "otherness" with respect to that [universal].
And this specific quality is a substitute for difference, not difference itself.

Furthermore, even in the absence of actual difference, it is the cause of the conventional usage of the relation between property and property-possessor (*dharma-dharmin-bhāva*) and so forth, which is the effect of difference.
The existence of being (*sattā*), the distinctness of the existent (*satī bhedaḥ*), and the fact that time exists at all times (*kālaḥ sarvadāsti*) and so forth are recognized by the learned;

this is established both through the impossibility of explaining such cognitions otherwise (*tat-pratīty-anyathānupapattyā*) and by the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which says, "Seeing the attributes as separate, he follows after them alone.
For here, having denoted the attributes of Brahman, their difference [from it] is negated.

Indeed, if even that representative of difference were absent, it would not be possible to speak of the relationship between attribute and substrate or the multiplicity of attributes; therefore, these points must be accepted even by those who do not wish to do so.
These matters should be investigated in their proper places within this treatise.
For here, the essential natures of the individual self (*jīvātman*), the supreme self (*paramātman*), their abode, and the means for attaining them are described exactly as they are.

In this context, the true nature of the Supreme Self is taught for the sake of understanding the true nature of the individual self; primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth are taught as the instruments of the Supreme Self, who is the creator, for the sake of His worship.
Furthermore, the means to that [worship] are threefold, distinguished as action (*karman*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and devotion (*bhakti*).
Among these, [the path of action] consists of that which is performed without regard for the various fruits mentioned in scripture and with the abandonment of attachment to agency.
Because one's own prescribed action (karma) assists knowledge and devotion by means of purifying the heart, it serves as an indirect means for attaining them;
and among those, the action prescribed by the Śruti that is free from violence is primary in this context.

In the *Mokṣadharma*, because of the dialogues between father and son and others, [the path] involving violence is secondary due to its remoteness, whereas for those two [the paths of knowledge and devotion], suchness is indeed direct.
Now, one might ask: when liberation is attained through the arising of knowledge via the purification of the heart by means of action performed in that manner, what is the distinction of devotion?
It is said: knowledge itself becomes devotion through a certain specific excellence.

The distinction between the two faces—one with unblinking vision and the other with side-long glances—is that the former is realized as the embodiment of consciousness (*cid-vigraha*), which constitutes *jñāna* (knowledge); through that, one attains states such as *sālokya*.

However, the realization of Him as the locus of the essence of His diverse divine sports (*līlā-rasa*) is *bhakti* (devotion); the human goal attained through this devotion is the acquisition of bliss, wherein states like *sālokya* are embraced and surpassed.

That devotion possesses the nature of knowledge is established by the scriptural text: "He abides in the yoga of devotion, whose sole flavor is existence, consciousness, and bliss" (*sac-cid-ānandaika-rase bhakti-yoge tiṣṭhati*).
This very [knowledge] is observed to be designated by such terms as "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) and "existence" (*bhāva*).
We shall explain that the nature of knowledge as having the form of hearing and so forth is to be understood as being like the locks of hair and other attributes of Viṣṇu, who is Cit-sukha.

In this scripture consisting of six triads, by the first triad there is a presentation of the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is a portion of the Lord, which is conducive to devotion toward the Lord, the whole.
And that [devotion] is described as being accomplished through internal knowledge and desireless action (*niṣkāma-karma*).

By the middle [section], devotion—which leads to the attainment of the Supreme Lord, the possessor of parts (*aṃśin*) who is the ultimate goal—is declared to be preceded by the knowledge of His majesty.
But by the final [section], the essential natures of the previously mentioned subjects, such as the Lord and others, are refined.
The designation of the three groups of six as being preceded by action, devotion, and knowledge is indeed according to their respective predominance.
The mention of both devotion and practice in the final [group] follows the analogy of the inscription on the lid of a jewel casket indicating its contents.
The qualified candidate for this treatise is one who possesses faith, is steadfast in the true Dharma, and has conquered the senses.
And that [devotion] is threefold, distinguished as being with expectation (*sa-niṣṭha*), fully perfected (*pariniṣṭhita*), and independent (*nirapekṣa*).

Among these, the first is one who, desiring even to behold the worlds such as heaven, practices his own duties in the form of worshiping Hari out of a sense of necessity (*niṣṭhayā*). The second is one who, desiring to sustain the world, practices those same duties while being devoted to devotion for Hari (*hari-bhakti-nirata*).
He and he [are the first two];
the third is without an āśrama, his mind purified by truth, austerity, recitation, and so forth, and solely devoted to Hari.
The relationship is that of the signified and the signifier.
The expressed object (*vācya*) is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, characterized as previously described; the expressive word (*vācaka*) is the scripture of His Gītā, which is of a corresponding nature;
and the purpose (*prayojana*) is the direct realization of Him preceded by the cessation of all afflictions—thus constitutes the fourfold preliminary connection (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*).
In this context, among the three beginning with Īśvara, the word *brahman* and the word *akṣara* [are used]; the word *kṣara* refers to the bound souls (*baddha-jīva*) and their bodies;
the word *ātman* is used for the body of Īśvara, the individual soul (*jīva*), the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and effort (*yatna*);
and the word *prakṛti* is used for the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), as well as for character (*śīla*) and essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The word *bhāva* is taught in the senses of existence, intention, intrinsic nature, category, birth, action, and self;
and the word *yoga* is recited in the sense of the three beginning with karma (object, etc. and the cessation of mental fluctuations.
Indeed, this treatise is the direct word of the Blessed One himself, the most excellent of all.

"The Gītā should be well-recited; what is the use of other extensive scriptures, since it has issued forth from the lotus-mouth of Padmanābha himself"—thus from the *Padma Purāṇa*. As for the speech of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and others, however, it was composed by Dvaipāyana for the sake of providing a context for it.
And that [world] is composed of that [consciousness], according to the maxim of falling into a salt-mine; this is the introduction.
As for the dialogue that took place between Govinda and Pārtha at the head of the battle:
To facilitate that association, the Sage first related the discourse found in the Gītās.
Thus, in order to introduce the dialogue between the Blessed One and Arjuna,
the narrative is set forth in twenty-seven verses beginning with "On the field of dharma" (*dharmakṣetre*).
Regarding this, it is said that Dhṛtarāṣṭra, knowing the Blessed One’s role as the charioteer for Pārtha yet doubting his own son’s victory, questioned Sañjaya.
To Janamejaya, Vaiśampāyana related that Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:

"Desirous of battle, wishing to fight, my sons and the Pāṇḍavas assembled at Kurukṣetra; what did they do? If it is objected: "Since you yourself have stated that they were 'desirous of battle' and 'assembled,' they would surely have fought; why then do you ask again, 'what did they do'? What is your intention? [The answer is as follows:]
Regarding this, he says: "In the field of dharma.

Based on such scriptural declarations as, "Kurukṣetra is indeed the field of dharma, the sacrificial ground of the gods, and the abode of Brahman for all beings," Kurukṣetra is well known as a soil in which dharma sprouts.
By its power, my sons—having had their enmity destroyed—resolved to give that kingdom to the Pāṇḍavas.

Or rather, did the Pāṇḍavas, who are always virtuous by nature, fearing unrighteousness caused by the destruction of their lineage in that field of dharma, consider entering the forest alone to be better?
"O Sañjaya"—the meaning is: through the grace of Vyāsa, you whose passion and hatred have been destroyed, speak the truth.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s failure to refer to the Pāṇḍavas as his own reveals his malice toward them.

Just as from a field of grain there is the removal of its adversaries, the mere semblances of grain, so too from the field of Dharma there will be the departure of your sons, who are its adversaries and mere semblances of Dharma; this is what is suggested by the Goddess of Speech through the term "field of Dharma. //1//
BhG 1.2 Sañjaya said:
Then, having seen the Pandava army drawn up in battle array, Duryodhana—
Having approached the teacher, the king spoke these words.

Śrīdhara: "Having seen," and so forth. Having seen the army (*anīkam*) of the Pāṇḍavas—meaning the host (*sainyam*)—arrayed, that is, stationed in a military formation (*vyūha-racanayā*), King Duryodhana approached the teacher Droṇa and spoke the words that are about to be related. (2)
Viśvanātha: Having understood his intention, [Kṛṣṇa] thought that the battle desired by him would indeed take place;
however, considering it to be contrary to his own wishes, he spoke after seeing [the army], saying "arrayed" (vyūḍha), meaning stationed in a military formation.
King Duryodhana, inwardly filled with fear, said:
"Behold this," in nine verses. //2//

Baladeva said: "Thus, having understood the state of mind of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—who is blind by birth, whose eye of wisdom has been destroyed, who is blinded by delusion through the loss of his sense of dharma, and whose heart is withered by the thought that 'my son might one day give that kingdom to the Pāṇḍavas'—the most righteous Sañjaya declared: 'Your son will never, under any circumstances, hand over the kingdom to them.'"

To generate satisfaction in him, he says "Having seen" (*dṛṣṭvā*). Having approached the army (*anīkam*) of the Pāṇḍavas— the troops stationed in a battle formation (*vyūha-racanayā*)— the King, who was himself skilled in royal policy (*rāja-nīti*), went personally into the presence of the Teacher (*ācāryam*), Droṇa, the bestower of the science of archery, and spoke words characterized by brevity of syllables, profundity of meaning, and a specific quality of transition in speech.

Here, by his coming personally into the presence of the Teacher, his internal fear—caused by witnessing the power of the Pāṇḍava army—is revealed; yet, through his reverence for his Guru, he conceals that fear by saying, "I have come here in person. Furthermore, this is due to his skill in royal policy (*rāja-nīti-naipuṇya*), as indicated by the word "king" (*rāja*). (2)
"Behold, O Teacher, this vast army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, drawn up in battle array by the wise son of Drupada, your own disciple. (BhG 1.3)

Śrīdhara: He expresses that very same speech through nine verses beginning with "Behold this" (*paśyaitām*). Regarding the word "Behold" (*paśya*), etc.: O Teacher, behold this great, vast army (*camū*)—the host—of the Pāṇḍavas.
It was formed by your disciple Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Drupada, and maintained through the arrangement of the battle formation. //3//

Viśvanātha: Although you knew that this [Dhṛṣṭadyumna], the son of Drupada and your own disciple, had been born for the purpose of slaying you, you nevertheless taught him; thus, your intellect is dull.

By the word "intelligent" (dhīmataḥ), the sense is that even from an enemy such as you, he acquired the knowledge of the means to slay you; observe his great intelligence even at the time of the final result. //3//
Baladeva: He spoke those words, beginning with "Behold her," and so forth.

Out of excessive affection for his dear disciples, Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, the Teacher thought, "He might not fight," and thus, in order to provoke his anger, he spoke while manifesting a slight disregard for him, saying "Behold her. Having seen her standing there, having disregarded both the Teacher who is very close by and you who are exceedingly brave through your audacity, perceive that disregard of yours.
"Arrayed" means established through the formation of a battle array.
"By the son of Drupada" refers to Drupada, your enemy; for it was said that Dhṛṣṭadyumna was produced from the sacrificial fire-pit by Drupada for the sake of slaying you.
"By your disciple" implies that even though you knew him to be your own enemy, you taught him the science of archery—this demonstrates your dull-wittedness.
"By the wise one"—that is, by the enemy—your means of destruction was grasped from you; thus his wisdom is [demonstrated].
"Only acting out of consideration for you" is the cause of our misfortune. //3//
Here [on our side] were heroes, great archers equal to Bhīma and Arjuna in battle—Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great chariot-warrior (mahāratha). //4//
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, the heroic King of Kāśī, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaibya, that bull among men; //5//
And Yudhāmanyu, the valiant, and the heroic Uttamaujas,
as well as the son of Subhadrā and the sons of Draupadī— all of them were indeed great chariot-warriors (mahāratha).
Śrīdhara: "In this," and so forth. "In this" means in this army (*camū*). "Arrows" (*iṣavaḥ*) are *bāṇāḥ*. "Bows" (*iṣāsāḥ*) are those by which these arrows are shot.
Those who are great archers are called *maheṣvāsas*.
Bhīma and Arjuna are already world-renowned as warriors here;
there are heroes equal to them, endowed with valor and the duty of a Kṣatriya.
He points them out by their names: Yuyudhāna Sātyaki; furthermore, Dhṛṣṭaketu;
and the one named Yudhāmanyu, who is valiant.
Saubhadra is Abhimanyu; the Draupadeyas are the five sons born to Draupadī from the five [Pāṇḍavas], Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, beginning with Prativindhya.
The definition of a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) and so forth is as follows:
"He who can fight ten thousand archers alone..."
And he who is proficient in both weapons and treatises is known as Mahārtha.
"He who would fight against immeasurable [enemies] is declared an *atiratha*;
he who would fight with even one [such enemy] is considered less than that, an *ardharatha*. //4-6//
Viśvanātha: Here, in the *caṇvām* [verse],
"those whose bows (*iṣvāsa*)— meaning their bows— are great, being impossible for enemies to cut," refers to Yuyudhāna, that is, Sātyaki.
Saubhadra is Abhimanyu.
The sons of Draupadī, such as Prativindhya and others, were born from the five [Pāṇḍavas] beginning with Yudhiṣṭhira.
The definition of a great chariot-warrior (mahāratha) and so forth is as follows:
He who can fight ten thousand archers alone and is proficient in both weaponry and treatises is known as a Mahārtha.
"He who can fight against immeasurable numbers is declared an *atiratha*;
he who can fight against one [such warrior] is considered slightly inferior, an *ardharatha*. (4–6)
Śrīdhara: If it be argued that "since this small army commanded by Dhrṣṭadyumna alone could be easily conquered by even one of our own, you need not fear," he says "atra" (here) in response.
Here, in this army, there are great archers whose bows cannot be cut by enemies.
Anticipating the objection regarding their skill in battle, he says "bhīma" (terrible).
Yuyudhāna Sātyaki is [the subject] for the three beginning with Mahāratha; "bull among men" (nara-puṅgava) is for the three beginning with Purujit.
"Valiant in battle" refers to Yudhāmanyu;
"possessed of heroism" refers to Uttamaujas—these are the epithets.
Saubhadra is Abhimanyu.
The sons of Draupadī—namely Prativindhya, Śrutasena, Śrutakīrti, Śatānīka, and Śrutakarman—are the five sons born of Draupadī from the five [Pāṇḍavas] beginning with Yudhiṣṭhira, respectively.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), others such as Ghaṭotkaca and so forth are also included;
however, the Pāṇḍavas themselves are not enumerated here because they are already too well known.
Those who have been counted as these seventeen,
and whoever else belongs to that faction— all of them are indeed great car-warriors (mahārathas).
This is also an illustration for the *atiratha*;
its definition has been stated thus:
"He who can make ten thousand archers fight alone [is an *atiratha*]."
And being proficient in both weapons and treatises, he is known as Mahārtha.
"He who fights against immeasurable [enemies] is declared an *atiratha*;
he who can fight even one [such enemy] is considered slightly inferior, an *ardharatha*. (4–6)
But as for those who are distinguished among us, learn of them, O best of the twice-born; I shall name them to you for the sake of your information, as they are the leaders of my army. (7)
Śrīdhara: "Asmākam" means "of us. "Nibodha" means "understand" or "be aware. "Nāyakāḥ" means "leaders" or "guides."
For the sake of conceptualization and for the sake of right knowledge. //7//
Viśvanātha: Understand—that is, become awakened—for the sake of recognition, that is, for the sake of perfect knowledge. //7//

Baladeva: "In that case, are you afraid of the Pāṇḍava army?"—anticipating this thought regarding his status as a teacher, and concealing even the fear born within him, he speaks with boldness, saying, "Of us.

"Among all of us, those who are distinguished, most excellent, leaders and guides endowed with the strength of intelligence and so forth—I speak of them for the sake of recognition, that is, for the sake of right knowledge."

If you do not fight because of your affection for the Pāṇḍavas, even then my victory will surely be achieved through Bhīṣma and the others; this is what should be made clear in order to provoke his anger. //7//

"You, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa who is victorious in assembly, Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, Saumadatti, and Jayadratha—[all these stand here]. (BhG 1.8) [And: "Droṇa, the preceptor, and his son, as well as Śalya, O best of charioteers. (BhG 1.9)
Moreover, many other heroes have surrendered their lives for my sake;
they carry various weapons and missiles, and all are experts in warfare. (9)
Śrīdhara: He addresses them with these two verses beginning with "bhavān. "Bhavān" refers to Droṇa;
he is so called because he conquers (jayati) the assembly (samitim), that is, the battle.
The son of Somadatta is Bhūriśravas;
"and others" means they have resolved to give up their lives for my sake—that is, for the purpose of my objective.
They are those who possess various—that is, many—weapons, which are the instruments of striking.
"Skilled in battle" means they are proficient [in it]. //8-9//
Viśvanātha: Saumadatti is Bhūriśravas.

"Having abandoned their lives" means that they were prepared even to give up their lives if it would result in my benefit; however, in reality, these men were already slain by me alone. As the Blessed One said, "Be merely an instrument, O Savyasācin," Duryodhana’s speech was indeed the truth. (8–9)
Baladeva said: "As for 'you'—you are Droṇa;
Vikarṇa is my younger brother."
"Saumadatti Bhūriśravas, Samitiñjaya, and Saṃgrāmavijayin"—these are the epithets for the seven [warriors] beginning with Droṇa.
[An objection: "But are there not only these many distinguished ones in my army? To which he replies, "And others," indicating that they are indeed innumerable.

"Many," such as Jayadratha, Kṛtavarman, Śalya, and others—"having abandoned," etc.—the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used here in the sense of the object; the meaning is that they have resolved to give up their lives.
And thus, because of their excessive affection for me, their extraordinary heroism, and their skill in battle, it is indicated that my victory will surely be achieved. (8–9)
"That army of ours, protected by Bhīṣma, is insufficient; but this army of theirs, protected by Bhīma, is sufficient. (10)
Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says: "It was insufficient," and so forth.
Even though our army—that is, our force—was joined by such heroes and protected by Bhīṣma, it appeared "insufficient," meaning it was incapable of fighting with them.
This army of the Pāṇḍavas, protected by Bhīma, appears truly sufficient and capable.
Because Bhīṣma is partial toward both sides, our army is incapable against the Pāṇḍava host;
but because Bhīma is partial toward only one side, the strength of the Pāṇḍavas is capable. //10//
Viśvanātha: "Inadequate" means incomplete;
the sense is that [the army] was incapable of fighting with the Pāṇḍavas.
Even though it was protected on all sides by Bhīṣma—who possessed extremely subtle intellect and was proficient in the science of weapons—it was so because Bhīṣma was partial toward both sides.

By Bhīma, however, who possesses a coarse intellect, these Pāṇḍavas—even though he himself is unacquainted with weapons and treatises—have been protected; that is to say, they have been made fully competent and complete for battle with us. //10//

Baladeva: Anticipating the objection—"Since the two armies are equal, how can victory belong to you alone?"—he states the superiority of his own forces with the words "insufficient" (*aparyāptam*). Our army is not only immeasurable (*aparimita*), but it is also protected by Bhīṣma, a man of great intelligence and a *mahāratha*.
The strength of these Pāṇḍavas is limited and finite;
moreover, it is protected by Bhīma, who is of meager intellect and a mere half-chariot warrior.
Therefore, my victory is assured. (10)
And in all the divisions, stationed each according to his respective position,
may you all indeed protect Bhīṣma alone. (11)

Viśvanātha: Therefore, he says that you must remain vigilant: "In the *ayanas*—the paths for entering the battle arrays—you, being divided according to your respective positions, must remain stationed without abandoning your own individual sectors of the battlefield; thus protect Bhīṣma from all sides so that, while he is fighting with others, he is not struck from behind by anyone."
The implication is that our very lives depend solely upon Bhīṣma’s strength. //11//

Baladeva: Now, if the Teacher, having understood the intent of my speech, should remain indifferent, then my mission would fail; perceiving this, and entrusting the burden of his own task to him, he says: "In the marches...

and so forth. In the marches—that is, on the paths for the entry of the army—they remained stationed, not abandoning their respective battlefields which had been divided according to their allotted portions.

"O sirs, Bhīṣma and those like you must protect him on all sides from the onset of battle; the meaning is that you should act so that no one else may strike him down when he cannot see his flanks or his rear.
For when Bhīṣma is the commander-in-chief, my victory is assured"—this is the intention.
This is the intention: Bhīṣma is our paternal grandfather, while you are our preceptor;
both of you are known to be those who desire our exclusive welfare.

"Even though they knew my injustice in the assembly hall and were questioned by Draupadī regarding her own justice, they did not speak; however, I informed them in such a way as to make them abandon their feigned affection for the Pāṇḍavas. (11)
Gladdening his heart, the powerful grandfather, the elder of the Kurus, uttered a lion’s roar and blew his conch shell loudly. (12)
Śrīdhara: Having heard these words of the king, which were full of great honor, what did Bhīṣma do?
To this he says, beginning with "tasya" (of him).
Making the king joyful, the grandfather Bhīṣma uttered a loud, great lion-roar and blew his conch shell—that is, he sounded it. (12)

Viśvanātha: Thereupon, the elder of the Kurus, Bhīṣma—feeling joy at hearing of his own honor and desiring to produce joy in Duryodhana by destroying his worldly existence (bhava)—uttered a "lion's roar" (*siṃhanāda*). [The grammatical form] *ṇamul* is used here according to the rule *upamāne karmaṇi ca*;
thus, the meaning is "having roared like a lion. //12//
Baladeva: Having thus perceived the self-praise offered by Duryodhana, Bhīṣma, filled with joy, blew his conch shell in order to dispel the fear born within him; so he says.

The suffix *ṇamul* is used here according to Pāṇini’s rule "siṃha-nādam" (Pāṇ. 3.4.48), which prescribes it for both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the action (*karman*); the meaning is that it is also used when the agent (*kartṛ*) is the object of comparison.

The meaning is "roaring like a lion. By not saying anything at all with his mouth, but merely sounding the conch shell, he indicates: "Victory and defeat indeed depend on the Lord; for your sake, I shall abandon my body according to the duty of a Kṣatriya" (BhG 1.13).
Then conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and horns were suddenly sounded; that noise became tumultuous.
Śrīdhara: Thus, having observed the battle-festival of the commander-in-chief Bhīṣma, the battle-festival proceeded everywhere; this he expresses with the words beginning with "tataḥ" (then).
*Paṇavas* are small drums (*mārdalas*);
*ānakas* and *gomukhas* are specific types of musical instruments.
Instantly, at that very moment, the musical instruments were struck;
and that tumultuous sound of conchs and other instruments became great. //13//
Viśvanātha: Then he says "tataḥ" (thereupon) to indicate that enthusiasm for battle arose on both sides;
*paṇavas* are small drums (*mārdalas*), and *ānakas* are kettledrums (*paṭahas*).
Gomukhas are specific types of musical instruments. //13//
Baladeva: Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then):
when Bhīṣma had set out as the commander-in-chief, at that very moment, suddenly, the conch shells and other instruments were sounded—that is, they were played.
This is a grammatical construction where the object functions as the agent (*karmakartari*).
The three types of musical instruments, beginning with the *paṇava*, produced a tumultuous sound that was great due to its uniformity of form. //13//
Then, stationed upon a great chariot yoked with white horses, Mādhava and the son of Pāṇḍu blew their divine conch shells. (14)

Śrīdhara: Then, with the five verses beginning with "tataḥ," he describes the enthusiasm for battle that arose in the Pāṇḍava army. Following the tumultuous noise of the Kaurava army's musical instruments, Śrī-Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, standing upon a great chariot (*syandana*), blew their divine conch shells (*śaṅkha*) with great force.
Viśvanātha: [No commentary].
Baladeva: Now, with the words "Then," he describes the festival of battle that commenced in the Pāṇḍava army.

Although it was true that others were also stationed on chariots, the specific mention of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna being on a chariot indicates that their chariot had been given by Agni, its capacity to conquer the three worlds, and its great majesty (BhG 1.15–18).
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya the Devadatta, and Vṛkodara, the performer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra. 15.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, [possessed] the Anantavijaya;
Nakula and Sahadeva [possessed] the Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka [conchs]. 16.
Kāśya, the supreme archer; Śikhaṇḍin, the great chariot-warrior;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna; Virāṭa; and the unconquered Sātyaki. //17//
O lord of the earth, Drupada, the sons of Draupadī, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, all blew their conch shells individually. 18.
Śrīdhara: Showing that very point through its divisions, he says "Pāñcajanya" and so forth.
Pāñcajanya and the others are the names of the conchs of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa and the rest.
Bhīma is one whose deeds are terrible (ghora).
He whose belly was like that of a wolf was Vṛkodara; he blew the great conch Pauṇḍra.
With the words "O Infinite One," Nakula blew the conch named Sughoṣa.
Sahadeva [is the author] of the work named Maṇipuṣpaka;
and there is also Kāśya— Kāśya being the King of Kāśī.
Of what nature was he? He was the supreme, most excellent archer (*iṣvāsa*), one whose bow was [such]; thus [he was called] Drupada.
O Lord of the Earth, Dhṛtarāṣṭra! //15-18//

Viśvanātha: *Pāñcajanya* and so forth are the names of the conch shells and other items. *Aparājita* means "unconquerable" because he cannot be defeated by anyone; alternatively, it means "resplendent" (*rājita*) with his bow (*cāpa*). //15–18//
Baladeva: "Pāñcajanya," and so forth—these are the names of the conchs of Kṛṣṇa and others.
Here, by the word *hṛṣīkeśa*, his being assisted by the Supreme Lord is indicated;
by the words *pāñcajanya* and the rest, his possession of many divine conchs with well-known names is indicated.

By these epithets— "King," "One of Terrible Deeds," and "Dhanañjaya"— the excellence of the Pāṇḍava army is indicated through Yudhiṣṭhira’s performance of the Rājasūya sacrifice, Arjuna’s slaying of Hiḍimba and others, and Bhīma’s acquisition of infinite wealth from his conquest of the quarters;
and by contrast, the inferiority of the enemy armies is shown through their lack of such qualities.
"Kāśya" refers to Kāśya, the King of Kāśi;
he was a supreme archer and a great bearer of the burden.

And the invincible one, radiant with his bow—O Drupada, O lord of the earth, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra! Thus it is indicated that the calamity arising from your evil counsel, characterized by the destruction of the lineage, is, in brief, imminent. (15–18)
That tumultuous roar, making both the sky and the earth resound, tore apart the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. (19)
Śrīdhara: And that sound of your conchs produced great fear; thus he says, "That roar," and so forth.
It shattered—that is, it tore apart—the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who were your enemies.
What was it doing?
Resounding with echoes, the tumultuous noise filled both the sky and the earth. //19//
Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: "Sa" (He).
The blast of the conch shell sounded by the Pāṇḍavas rent asunder the hearts of all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, including Bhīṣma and the others.
The meaning is that it produced a pain equal to the tearing apart of those [ear-rings].
"Tumulo" means extremely intense; "abhyanunādayan" means resounding on all sides with echoes.

It should be understood that although the noise made by the Dhārtarāṣṭras with their conchs and other instruments was tumultuous, it did not produce even the slightest agitation in them, because it is not described as such. //19//
Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra drawn up in battle array and as the discharge of weapons was about to begin, the Pāṇḍava whose banner bears the monkey raised his bow. (1.20)
Śrīdhara: At this time, Arjuna addressed Śrī Kṛṣṇa; this he states in the four verses beginning with "atha.
The word "atha" means "thereafter"; "vyavasthitān" means those standing ready for the exertion of battle;
"kapidhvajaḥ" refers to Arjuna. //20//

Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: Having thus demonstrated the fear of the Dhārtarāṣṭras regarding battle, he speaks of the enthusiasm of the Pāṇḍavas with the following one and a half verses, beginning with "atha. "Then" (*atha*) means immediately after the breaking of their enthusiasm caused by the sound of the enemy's conch; "stationed" (*vyavasthitān*) means standing ready with the desire to fight, which opposes that breaking of enthusiasm.

The meaning is that Arjuna, whose banner bears the monkey, is favored by Hanumān— that great hero by whom even the great deeds of the illustrious son of Daśaratha were accomplished in the past— and is thus entirely free from even the scent of fear;
O Lord of the Earth, while [the battle] has commenced and is currently proceeding.
"Hṛṣīkeśam" means Hṛṣīkeśa, Kṛṣṇa, the impeller of all the senses; he spoke these words.
The sense is that for those Pāṇḍavas—who are His exclusive devotees and for whom Hari, the Lord of All, is their servant—there is not even a scent of doubt regarding their victory. //20//
Then, O Lord of the Earth, he spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa:
"O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies. (1.21)
While I was observing these warriors standing there, desirous of battle, [I wondered]: "With whom among them must I fight in this undertaking of war? (22)
I behold those who have gathered here,
desiring to do what is pleasing in battle to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as they prepare for combat.

Śrīdhara explains that very statement beginning with "of both armies" and so forth, up to "these. [An objection is raised: "But you are a warrior, not a spectator of the battle. To this he replies with "by whom with me," and so forth.
"With whom must I fight?

I wish to see those who have assembled here desiring to do what is pleasing to Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son Duryodhana—those who are about to fight. Until that time, station my chariot between the two armies. This is the syntactical connection [of the verses 21–23].

Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: He speaks Arjuna’s words beginning with "senayoḥ": "O Acyuta, you do not fall away from your natural perfection of affection for devotees nor from your supreme sovereignty."
"Driven by my word, take my chariot to each respective place where my food is located; establish the chariot there without fear.
Regarding the fruit of establishing the chariot there, he says "yāvat" (as many as...).
[He refers to those] desiring to fight, but not those wishing to make peace with us.
[He stood] firm, not wavering out of fear.
If it is asked, "But you are a warrior, not a spectator of battle; so what is the point of looking at them?", he says [the answer] with the word "by whom" (kaiḥ).

"The reason for stationing the chariot in the midst [of the two armies] was precisely to gain this knowledge: 'In this mutual exertion of my kinsmen toward battle, with which kinsmen will my own battle take place?

One might object: 'Surely, because of their kinship, they will simply arrange for peace. To that he replies: 'Those who are about to fight'—meaning those who will not arrange for peace—I observe, that is, I recognize."
This refers to one who is evil-minded, dull-witted, and ignorant of the means for his own livelihood, but not to the removal of that evil mind through battle.
Therefore, it is appropriate to observe the opponent in my battle. //21-23//
Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, having stationed that best of chariots between the two armies, [said: (24)
In the presence of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the rulers of the earth,
he said, "O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here."
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry, "What happened after that?", Sañjaya said, "Thus addressed," and so forth.
Being thus addressed by Arjuna—the lord (īśa) who has conquered sleep (nidrā)—who is called Uḍāka because of his sleep... [the Lord spoke].
"O Bhārata, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Hṛṣīkeśa has stationed that best of chariots between the two armies;
having placed the chariot in front of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and at the head of all the kings and rulers of the earth, the Blessed Lord said, 'O Pārtha, behold these Kurus. (24–25)

Viśvanātha: Although Hṛṣīkeśa is the controller of all the senses, he was thus addressed by Arjuna and commanded; the sense is that the Lord’s subjection to love is such that he became governable even by the mere organ of speech of Arjuna. By Guḍākeśa—just as *guḍā* (molasses) reveals only sweetness, so too his "hairless ones" (*akeśāḥ*), namely Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva, reveal the savor of his own rasa of affection; for he [Guḍākeśa] possesses them, where *a* is Viṣṇu and *ka* is... [Śiva].
Brahmā, Īśa, and Mahādeva—
wherein the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself, the crest-jewel of all incarnations, became subject to love and obedient to her command;
how could Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra, who are but partial incarnations (guṇāvatāras) of Him, manifest their own sovereignty there?
However, the meaning is that they consider themselves to have achieved their purpose only after manifesting the essence of affection originating from themselves.
As it was said by the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Supreme Abode: "I desire to see you two, who are born of my own self as brahmins.
Alternatively, *guḍāka* means sleep; thus, it means "by the master of sleep," i.e., by one who has conquered sleep.

In this commentary as well, the sense is: what wonder is there that even Māyā—who is herself the direct controller of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—was conquered and brought under control by that Arjuna through his love, whereby even poor old sleep, which is a manifestation of Māyā, was defeated?
[This occurred] in the presence of Bhīṣma and Droṇa, and before all the rulers of the earth.
The word "pramukhataḥ" is drawn forward [to the subsequent clause], even though it has already entered into the compound. //24-25//
Baladeva: In response to the inquiry as to what occurred thereafter, Sañjaya said, "Thus.

Guḍākā means sleep; its Lord (Guḍākeśa) is one who has conquered sleep by fixing his mind on the remembrance of the qualities and beauty of his own friend, the Blessed Lord. Thus addressed and impelled by Arjuna—that supreme devotee—Hṛṣīkeśa, who knows the fluctuations of his mind, [acted].

The Blessed One, having stationed his supreme chariot—the chariot given by Agni—in the midst of the two armies, in front of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the rulers of the earth and kings, said: "O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here.
By the two words "Pārtha" and "Hṛṣīkeśa," this is indicated: because you are my maternal uncle's son and my father's sister's son, I shall act as your charioteer.
"I shall indeed do so; you, however, will abandon the desire to fight this very moment—what is the use of looking at the enemy's army?
This is the sense, expressed with irony. //24-25//
There, Pārtha saw standing his fathers and grandfathers,
as well as teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends.
As well as fathers-in-law and friends, on both sides of the two armies. //26//
Śrīdhara: To [answer] the question "What happened after that?", he says "There," and so forth. "Fathers" means paternal uncles.
"Sons and grandsons" means those who were the sons and grandsons of Duryodhana and the others.
He saw his friends (*sakhīn*), his companions (*mitrāṇi*), and his well-wishers (*suhṛdaḥ*) who had rendered him assistance;
Viśvanātha explains these as the sons and grandsons of Duryodhana and the others.
Baladeva: Regarding how Arjuna, having been thus addressed by the Blessed One, beheld the enemy army, he says [the following] in one and a half verses beginning with "There.
There, in that enemy army, he saw his fathers, such as Bhūriśravas and others;
his grandfathers, such as Bhīṣma, Somadatta, and others.
The teachers, such as Droṇa and Kṛpa; the maternal uncles, such as Śalya and Śakuni; and the brothers, such as Duryodhana and others.
Sons such as Lakṣmaṇa and others,
grandsons— that is, nephews— and the sons of Lakṣmaṇa and others.
"Friends" (sakhīn) refers to the sons of Droṇa, Jayadratha, and others;
"well-wishers" (suhṛdaḥ) refers to Kṛtavarman, Bhagadatta, and others.
This same principle should be understood to apply to one's own army as well.
Having observed all those stationed in both armies, according to the sequence [of the verse]. //26//
Beholding all those kinsmen standing there, that son of Kuntī,
overcome by supreme compassion and despondent, spoke this.
Śrīdhara: He states what Arjuna did next with the words "tān" (them).
Having thus observed both armies and being overcome by great compassion, Arjuna, becoming despondent, spoke these words.
This is the meaning of the sentence comprising the latter half of the verse.
"Possessed" means pervaded. //27//

Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: Now, the Lord of All, the compassionate Kṛṣṇa, desiring to uplift the universe by means of instruction regarding His own self along with His associates, sought to make Arjuna His disciple; however, [Arjuna] perceived even that battle—which was his own duty—as unrighteous, based on a semblance of the meaning of the Vedic injunction: "One should not harm any living beings."

Having manifested that delusion, he brought it about; thus he says, "O son of Kuntī, look at them," by declaring his own relationship as the son of his father’s sister, whereby his delusion and grief—characteristic of that [relationship]—are then revealed in him.
This is because it is stated that [the action] was performed out of compassion (*kṛpā*).
It will be shown that compassion is established by its very nature;

therefore, "supreme" (*parayā*) is its qualification. Alternatively, there is a division [of the compound] as "inferior" (*aparayā*); the meaning is that while compassion existed previously even toward one's own army, it now exists even toward the enemy army.

"Despairing," "repentant," and "finding"—since the expression of despair and the expression [of these states] occur at the same time, at the moment of speaking, the effects of despair, such as tears, trembling, and a choked throat, are manifested. //27//
O Kṛṣṇa, seeing these kinsmen standing here desiring to fight,
my limbs fail me and my mouth is parched. (28)
Trembling comes over my body and my hair stands on end; the Gāṇḍīva slips from my hand and my skin itself burns. (29)
Śrīdhara: In response to the expectation of what he said, he says "Having seen these," and so forth, up to the end of the chapter.
O Kṛṣṇa, having seen my own kinsmen—my relatives—standing arrayed before me desiring to fight, my limbs, such as my hands and feet, fail and dissolve. Furthermore, "and they tremble," and so forth.
Trembling is shaking;
horripilation is the bristling of the hair;
"he falls" means he collapses.
He is burned on all sides and tormented. //28–29//
Viśvanātha: Regarding the word "dṛṣṭvā" (having seen), the word "sthitasya" (of one who stands) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. //28-29//

Baladeva: He repeats what the son of Kuntī said while overwhelmed by grief, beginning with the words "Having seen this... (2.1). "Svajana" refers to one's own circle of kinsmen; as Amara states: "Sagotra, bāndhava, jñāti, bandhu, sva, and svajana are synonyms.

Having seen them, the limbs of me—who am standing here—namely the hands, feet, and so forth, fail and waste away, becoming parched. This indicates that the present wasting is more intense than the kind caused by mere physical exhaustion.
Trembling is a shaking;
horripilation is bristling of the hair.
By the dropping of the Gāṇḍīva bow, his lack of fortitude is shown, and by the burning of the skin, the burning of his heart is indicated. //28-29//
And I am unable to stand steady; my mind seems to reel, O Keśava, and I behold adverse omens. (30)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "I am unable," and so forth;
I perceive adverse omens—inauspicious signs that indicate undesirable results. //30//
Viśvanātha: "Adverse omens" (*viparītāni nimittāni*). Here, the word *nimitta* signifies "purpose" or "cause," as in the expression, "This residence of mine here is for the sake of wealth.

Therefore, the meaning is: since I am the victor in battle, there will be no happiness from the acquisition of a kingdom; rather, the opposite of that—namely, the suffering of remorse—will surely come to pass. //30//
Baladeva: "And even though" (*api ceti*) means that the mind wavers as if to remain steady; thus, there is the arising of weakness and fainting.
I perceive adverse omens and results here in this battle.
For me, the victor, there will be no attainment of the kingdom or joy, but rather its opposite—only remorse will come to pass.
The word *nimitta* denotes the result (*phala*), because in such instances as "For what purpose (*nimitta*) do you live here?", it is understood in that way. //30//
And I do not perceive any good in slaying my own kin in battle; I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. (1.31)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the words "And not," etc.:
I do not see any beneficial result from killing one's own kinsmen in battle—that is, in war.
If it is asked, "Do you not see results such as victory? he says in response: "I do not desire [them]. (31)
Viśvanātha: "I see no higher good than these two persons in this world who pierce the solar orb:
the wandering mendicant absorbed in yoga, and one slain facing the enemy in battle."

Because, by such statements as these, the prescription of the highest good (śreya) is made for one who has been slain, whereas for the slayer there is not even the slightest merit. [Objection: But is it not seen that the visible fruit of battle consists of fame or sovereignty? To this he says: "I do not desire" (na kāṅkṣe). //31//

Baladeva: Having thus described grief, which is contrary to the knowledge of reality, He speaks of the perverted intellect that is also contrary to it, beginning with "nor do I see" (*na ca*). [He says: "I do not see any good at all in killing one's own kinsmen in battle. "There are these two persons in the world who pierce the solar orb... [and so forth].
A wandering mendicant engaged in yoga, and one slain while facing the enemy in battle;
Because it is remembered that there is no spiritual welfare for the killer of one who has been slain by such means as these, there is no welfare whatsoever for me.

Alternatively, there is a word-break at *asvajanam* (not one's own kin); the meaning is that since there is no welfare even in the killing of those who are not one's kin, how much less so in the killing of one's own kin?
If it is argued that there is a visible result in the form of the acquisition of fame and kingdom, he says in response: "I do not desire it."

Since I am devoid of any longing for sovereignty and the like, my engagement in the means to victory is not appropriate, just as cooking is not for one who lacks a desire to eat. Therefore, dwelling in the forest alone will constitute our praiseworthy way of life. //31//
"Of what use is sovereignty to us, O Govinda, or of what use are enjoyments or even life itself—for whose sake we desire sovereignty, enjoyments, and pleasures? (32)
These who stand here in battle—teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers—have renounced both their lives and their wealth. (33)
Uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives—these I do not wish to kill, O Madhusūdana, even though they are killing me. (34)
Even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, how much less for the sake of the earth? O Janārdana, what joy could there be for us after slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra? (35)
Śrīdhara: He elaborates on this very point with the two and a half verses beginning with "What have we to do with kingdom? and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "these [men]":
those for whose sake our kingdom and other possessions were desired—having abandoned their lives and wealth and having accepted renunciation—they now stand ready for battle.
The meaning is: "Therefore, what use have we for kingdom and such things?
[Arjuna objects: "But if you do not slay them out of compassion, they will surely slay you out of greed for the kingdom;
therefore, you yourself should slay them and enjoy the kingdom."
Regarding this, he says "etān" and so forth in one and a half verses.
"Even these" means even those who strike us, even those who kill us; the word "api" (even) is used for emphasis.

Even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, or even for the purpose of attaining that, I do not wish to kill; how much less, then, for the sake of obtaining mere earth—this is the meaning. //32–35//
Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: "Govinda"—the meaning is: "O You who find (*vindasi*) the 'cows' (*gāḥ*), that is, the functions of all the senses; thus, understand what is in my mind."

He states the reason for the lack of desire for kingship and so forth with the words "of those who... The terms "life-breaths" (*prāṇān*) and "wealths" (*dhanāni*) should be understood through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as meaning the hope for life and the hope for wealth.

The sense is that even if one's own life were at stake, there might be a longing for kingship for the sake of the happiness of one's kinsmen; yet since even their destruction would occur in this [war], their engagement in battle is entirely purposeless.
If it is argued: "But if you are compassionate and do not kill them, then they will kill you yourself in order to make their own kingdom free of thorns," he says in response: "These.
Even though they are striking me and harming me, I do not wish to kill these people—even for the sake of attaining sovereignty over the three worlds, let alone for the sake of mere land.

If it is argued that one should abandon kinsmen and kill only the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, because happiness arises from the slaughter of those who have caused much suffering, to this he says: "Having slain" (nihatya).

For us Pāṇḍavas, standing here after having slain the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra such as Duryodhana and the rest, what joy or satisfaction could there be? None at all. [This is so] because, out of a longing for a brief flash of pleasure, one is deluded regarding the cause of long-lasting hell.
The sense is that [he] is not suitable [for this task].

By addressing him as "O Janārdana," it is suggested that if these are to be slain, then you alone, the remover of the earth's burden, must kill them; thus, it is implied that for you, the Supreme Lord, there can be no connection even with the slightest scent of sin. (32–35)
"By slaying these aggressors, we would only incur sin ourselves;
therefore, it is not right for us to kill the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, our own kinsmen."
For how, O Mādhava, could we be happy after killing our own kinsmen? (36)
Śrīdhara: But surely it is said: "The arsonist, the poisoner, one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the stealer of land or wife—these six are indeed *ātatāyin*s (assassins)."

According to this traditional teaching, these individuals are indeed *ātatāyins* (aggressors) by virtue of six causes, such as arson and so forth; and the killing of *ātatāyins* is entirely appropriate.
"One should kill an approaching *ātatāyin* without hesitation;
there is no fault whatsoever for the slayer in the killing of an *ātatāyin*."
Because of this statement, he says "only evil" and so forth in one and a half verses.
The passage beginning with "An assassin (ātatāyin) approaching... is an *artha-śāstra* (treatise on worldly affairs).
And that [custom] is weaker than the *dharma-śāstra*, as stated by Yājñavalkya: "In the conflict between two *smṛtis*, however, logic is stronger in legal proceedings;
but the *dharma-śāstra* is stronger than the *artha-śāstra*: such is the settled rule."

Thus, even in the case of killing these preceptors and others who are aggressors, only sin would accrue to us; for since this killing is unjust and unrighteous, there would be no happiness either here or in the hereafter. With this in mind, he says "one's own kin" (svajanam). //36//
Viśvanātha: Now, it is said: "The arsonist, the poisoner, one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the abductor of land or wife—these six are indeed *ātatāyin*s (aggressors)."
Thus:
"One should indeed slay an approaching assassin without hesitation;
there is no fault whatsoever for the slayer in the killing of an assassin."
From such statements as these, it follows that their slaughter is entirely appropriate. To this, he replies with the word "sin":
[even] having slain these who stand before us.
The treatise on worldly affairs (*artha-śāstra*), such as the rule regarding "an approaching assassin," is weaker than the treatise on dharma (*dharma-śāstra*).
As Yājñavalkya stated: "But it is traditionally held that the treatise on dharma is stronger than the treatise on worldly affairs."
Thus, there would certainly be sin in the killing of teachers and others, and there would not even be happiness in this world; therefore, he says "one's own kin" (svajanam). //36//
Baladeva: But surely, "The incendiary, the poisoner, one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the abductor of land or wife—these six are indeed assassins (ātatāyin)."
One should indeed slay an approaching assassin without hesitation;
there is no fault whatsoever for the slayer in the killing of an assassin.
If it is argued that, because of this statement, the killing of these six types of aggressors (*ātatāyin*) is justified, he replies with the word "sin" (*pāpam*).
By killing these who stand before us, only sin—which is the cause of the destruction of kinsmen—would attach to us.

The underlying point is this: the treatise on statecraft (*artha-śāstra*), which says "an approaching aggressor," etc., is weaker than the treatise on dharma (*dharma-śāstra*), which says "one must not harm any living beings."
But it is an established principle that the treatise on Dharma is more powerful than the treatise on Artha.
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti.
Therefore, by the force of the scripture which has a weak purpose, the slaughter of venerable persons such as Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and others, is indeed a cause of sin.
He concludes with the words "therefore" what was stated beginning with "And I do not see any good [in this]."
The meaning is: because of the possibility of evil, and because even bodily happiness is absent;
for indeed, without our teachers and kinsmen, [we have nothing].
The enjoyment of sovereignty, though it may lead to pleasure, will result only in regret;
the sense is: "O Mādhava! You are the Lord of Śrī, yet why do you engage in this battle which is devoid of glory? //36//
Even though these men, their minds overwhelmed by greed, do not perceive the evil resulting from the destruction of the family, nor the sin in betraying friends. (1.37)
O Janārdana, how could we not know how to turn away from this sin, when we clearly perceive the evil brought about by the destruction of our own kin? (38)

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But surely, since the fault of killing kinsmen is equal for you as well, just as these men proceed to battle even while accepting the fault of killing their kin, so too should you proceed;
why this despondency? To this he replies with two verses beginning with "Even though" (*yadyapi*).
Even though these men, Duryodhana and the others—whose minds are corrupted by greed for the kingdom and whose discrimination has fallen away—do not perceive the fault, [it is not so for me].
Nevertheless, since we perceive this fault, how could we not know how to turn away from this sin? The meaning is that one must apply the intellect solely toward such abstention. //37-38//
Viśvanātha: [Objection: "In that case, how then do these [beings] engage in battle? To this he says: "Even though... (37–38).

Indeed, it is the knowledge that an action is attended by a desired result that prompts one to act;
and that which is desired must be stated as being connected with what is undesired. As it has been said:
"Furthermore, that action which, even in its result, is followed by various undesirable consequences..."
"Because it is the cause of pure joy alone, it is called dharma.

Thus, even though this battle is enjoined by scripture—as in the injunction "One seeking to practice sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena"—our engagement in this war is not proper, because, like the Śyena and other such rites, it is followed by undesirable consequences.
However, the scriptural injunction beginning with "when summoned," etc., refers to future circumstances regarding living beings, provided that the fault of destroying one's lineage is absent.
"He [is called] Janārdana," as before. //37-38//
BhG 1.39: With the destruction of the family, the eternal family traditions perish. When the dharma is lost, unrighteousness overcomes the entire family. //39//

Śrīdhara: He points out that very same fault in the verse beginning with "In the destruction of the family" (*kula-kṣaye*). "Eternal" (*sanātanāḥ*) means those who have not attained one another [in marriage].
Furthermore, even the entire remaining family is overcome—that is, pervaded—by unrighteousness (*adharma*); this is the meaning. //39//

Viśvanātha: Regarding "the destruction of the family" (*kula-kṣaya*), the meaning is that [these traditions] have been obtained for a long time by being handed down from one generation to another within the family; thus they are called "eternal" (*sanātana*). //39//
Baladeva: He elaborates on the very fault [of war] with the words "destruction of the family" (*kula-kṣaya*).

The eternal family traditions (*kula-dharmāḥ*)—the duties appropriate to the family, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and others, handed down through successive generations—are destroyed because of the disappearance of their performer. The word "even" (*uta*), used here in the sense of "also," is connected with the word "entirely" (*kṛtsnam*).
The meaning is that when Dharma has perished, unrighteousness (adharma) overcomes the entire remaining family, including the children and others. //39//

O Kṛṣṇa, through the predominance of unrighteousness, the women of the family become corrupted; O Vārṣṇeya, when women are corrupted, there arises a mixture of the social orders (varṇasaṃkara). //40//
Śrīdhara: And therefore, [the verse begins] "From the overwhelming of unrighteousness," and so forth. //40//
Viśvanātha: "They become corrupted. The meaning is that it is unrighteousness (*adharma*) itself that impels them toward such transgression. //40//

Baladeva: "And then, due to the predominance of unrighteousness" means that the women of the family, struck by evil intent, would become corrupt, thinking: "Just as our husbands have transgressed dharma and engaged in the sin characterized by the destruction of the family, so too shall we disregard our wifely fidelity (pātivratya) and engage in misconduct. This is the meaning. //40//
The intermixture [of castes] leads only to hell for both the destroyers of the family and the family itself; indeed, their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water. (1.41)
Śrīdhara: "This being so, there is confusion," and so forth.
The ancestors of these destroyers of the family fall;
for they are those whose rites of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and water libations (udaka) have been interrupted.
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: The construction is that the corruption of the lineage leads the destroyers of the lineage to hell alone;
it is not only the destroyers of the lineage who fall into hell.
But he says that their fathers also [fall], for the word "hi" indicates the reason:
because the givers of the *paṇḍā* and so forth lack sons and other descendants, they—having lost the performance of the *piṇḍa*-offerings and other rites—fall indeed into hell. //41//
By these faults of the destroyers of the family, which cause the intermixture of castes, the eternal laws of the birth-group and the laws of the family are destroyed. (42)
Śrīdhara: He summarizes the aforementioned defect with two verses beginning with "doṣaiḥ. They are "uprooted," meaning they are destroyed.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the duties of birth, the duties of caste, and the duties of family," the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) and so forth are also included. //42//
Viśvanātha: "By defects" means they are uprooted or destroyed. //42//
Baladeva: With the two verses beginning with "doṣaiḥ," he summarizes the aforementioned defect.
They are "uprooted" (utsādyante), that is, destroyed;
the "caste-qualities" (jāti-dharmāḥ) are those based on the constraints of being a Kṣatriya and so forth.
But the duties of the family (kula-dharma) are non-common; by the word "and" (ca), the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) are to be understood. //42//
O Janārdana, we have heard from tradition that for those men who have destroyed the dharma of their lineage, residence in hell is inevitable. (1.43)

Śrīdhara: "Utsannā" means those whose family traditions (*kula-dharma*) have perished; this is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those whose caste traditions (*jāti-dharma*) have likewise perished. "Anuśuśruma" means we have heard it from tradition.
Men who do not perform expiation and remain devoted to sinful deeds go to terrible and agonizing hells, devoid of peace and remorse.
From such statements as these. //43//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: "Utsanna" (destroyed);
this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for caste, religious duties, and so forth.
We have heard from the mouth of our teacher that we who possess sacred learning:
men who, devoted to sins, do not perform expiation,
go to terrible and agonizing hells, devoid of peace and remorse.
By such statements as these. //43//
"Alas! What a great sin we are resolved to commit, that for the sake of the greed for the pleasures of a kingdom, we are prepared to slay our own kinsmen. (1.44)
Śrīdhara: Regarding the comparison [to the slaughter of one's own kin], he says "Alas! and so forth.
That we have resolved to commit this great sin—namely, that we have made the determination to kill our own kinsmen—"alas!
what great misery! is the meaning. //44//

Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: Even by the resolve to kill her kinsman, sin would be possible; therefore, she speaks what is inconsistent [with such a motive], beginning with "Aho! The particle *batā* expresses doubt. //44//
If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with weapons in hand, should slay me in battle while I am unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me. (1.45)
Śrīdhara: Being thus tormented and desiring only death, he says, "If they shall kill me," and so forth.
If they should kill me—who am sitting silently and without means of resistance—then that killing would be more secure for me, that is, extremely beneficial, because no sin would arise. //45//

Viśvanātha: Nothing. Baladeva: [Objection: "But even if you have desisted from the slaughter of kinsmen, Bhīṣma and the others, being eager for battle, will surely kill you; what then should be done? To this he says: "If me," and so forth.

It is without remedy; for there is no expiation for the sin of the resolve to kill me that has already been made. It is far better and more beneficial to remove this sin through the very act of giving up one's life.
The implication is that Bhīṣma and the others will certainly not suffer the fruit of that sin. //45//
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna sat down on the seat of the chariot,
casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry, "What happened after that?", Sañjaya said, beginning with the words "Having spoken thus," and so forth.
In the *saṅkhya*, meaning in the battle, he sat down—that is, he sat upon the seat of the chariot (*rathopastha*), which is on top of the chariot.
He was one whose mind and heart were agitated and trembling with grief. //46//
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Despair of Arjuna," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmin.

Viśvanātha: "In the battle" means in the conflict; "on the seat of the chariot" means upon the chariot. Thus [ends the commentary] in the *Sārārthavarṣiṇī*, which brings joy to the hearts of devotees.
The first chapter of the Gītā has been thoroughly reconciled with the views of the virtuous. 46.

Baladeva: In response to the inquiry, "What happened after that?", Sañjaya said, "Having spoken thus... He sat down—that is, he sat upon the seat of the chariot (rathopasthe), meaning on top of the chariot—having previously stood up for the sake of battle and for the purpose of looking for an opponent to fight.
In one who is non-violent and moistened with compassion, the desire to know the Self arises;
it does not arise at all in one who is its opposite—this has been established from the very beginning. (46)
